prompt_package.goal_summary: Put the same mascot or character into any new scene without the face or outfit drifting.

user_profile.who: Brand owner or illustrator building a recurring character

blocks.task: Place my character {{character_name}} in a new scene: {{scene_brief}}. The character must look identical to the attached reference images.
blocks.subject: {{character_name}}, {{age_and_type}}, wearing {{outfit}}. Same face shape, same eye spacing, same nose, same hairstyle, same body proportions as reference image 1. Same outfit colors and logo placement as reference image 2.
blocks.scene: {{scene_brief}}. The character is {{pose}} and {{action}}. Scene depth is clear, with foreground, subject and background separated.
blocks.camera: {{shot_type}}, character occupies about 60% of the frame height, three-quarter view, eye level.
blocks.light: {{light_mood}}, soft shadows, clear separation between character and background.
locks: Face, hairstyle and body proportions match reference image 1 exactly. Do not restyle the face.
Outfit, accessories and logo colors match reference image 2 exactly.
Overall art style matches reference image 3 exactly: same line weight, same shading, same palette.
avoid: changing age, ethnicity or body type
text or speech bubbles I did not request

input_schema.description: Use three reference images: face, outfit, style. More than three dilutes the signal.

fields.name: outfit
fields.example: mustard raincoat and a small canvas satchel

fields.name: scene_brief
fields.example: standing in a rainy bookshop doorway at dusk

fields.name: shot_type
fields.example: medium shot from the knees up

fields.name: light_mood
fields.example: warm shop light against cool blue rain

output_schema.description: The new scene plus a drift score you assign yourself.

examples.title: Mascot in a rainy bookshop doorway

example_input.scene_brief: standing in a rainy bookshop doorway at dusk

non_obvious_insights: Three references beat five. Face, outfit and style are different signals; extra images blur which one wins.
Describe the face in words too. Image references carry identity, but words stop the model from reinterpreting it.
Lock the line weight. The fastest visual drift is not the face, it is the drawing technique.
Keep a fixed 'character sheet' file with the face at the same crop and angle every time. Consistent input is half the consistency.
Change one variable per run. If you change scene and outfit together, you cannot tell which one broke the look.
Do not ask for a new expression and a new outfit in the same run. Expressions alter face geometry.
Save your best result as reference image 1 for the next run. The character sheet improves like a family photo album.
monetization_ideas: Sell a character bible service: 12 consistent scenes plus a reusable reference set.
Offer a children's book package: cover and 12 spreads with one locked character.
License mascot scene packs to small brands for seasonal campaigns.
Run a monthly 'mascot in the news' social pack for one client, same package, new scenes.
Sell the drift checklist as a QA document to studios that outsource illustration.
prompt_package.reusability_notes: Change art_style for a new brand and the package still works. Swap character for a product, a pet or a real person (with consent) and reuse the same locks. For animation-style turnarounds, set aspect_ratio to 16:9 and ask for four panels of the same character in one image, then cut them apart.
